passages.t: Three signs for a people who may not believe
passages.happening:
Moses answers, “What if they do not believe me or listen to my voice? For they may say, ‘The LORD has not appeared to you’” (verse 1).

God asks, “What is that in your hand?” “A staff,” Moses replies (verse 2). He throws it down and it becomes a snake, and he runs from it. God tells him to grab it by the tail, and it becomes a staff again (verses 3-4).

Then God tells him to put his hand inside his cloak. When he takes it out, “his hand was leprous, white as snow” (verse 6). He puts it back, and it comes out “restored, like the rest of his skin” (verse 7).

If they still do not believe, he is to pour Nile water on the ground, and “the water you take from the Nile will become blood on the ground” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
This is Moses' third objection. In 3:18 God said the elders would listen to him. Moses answers with the same words turned around: what if they do not listen?

God's answer starts with something ordinary: the shepherd's staff in Moses' hand. The three signs speak to Egypt in a way any Egyptian would understand. A rearing cobra sat on the front of Pharaoh's crown as a sign of royal and divine power. Many readers see the first sign as saying that the LORD holds that power by the tail. And picking up a snake by the tail is a good way to get bitten. Moses' obedience is a small act of trust.

The word for the diseased hand covers a range of skin diseases, not only what we now call leprosy. In Israel's later law such a disease made a person unable to take part in worship until healed (Leviticus 13 and 14). The sign shows that God can strike and God can heal. It touches Moses' own body.

The third sign touches the Nile, on which every Egyptian life depended. It is a preview of the first plague (7:17-21). Verse 8 speaks of the signs as if they had a voice. Signs speak too, alongside Moses' words.
passages.later:
The same picture, a hand ‘white as snow’, is used of Miriam when she is struck with the disease (Numbers 12:10).

Jesus' signs in John's Gospel are given for the same purpose as these: “these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name” (John 20:31).
passages.asks: God asked Moses, ‘What is that in your hand?’ and used an ordinary shepherd's staff. Ask what ordinary thing in your hand God might use: a skill, a job, a home, a little time. And ask whether you have been waiting for something grander before you will trust him with it.

passages.happening:
“Please, Lord,” Moses says, “I have never been eloquent, neither in the past nor since You have spoken to Your servant, for I am slow of speech and tongue” (verse 10).

God answers, “Who gave man his mouth? Or who makes the mute or the deaf, the sighted or the blind? Is it not I, the LORD? Now go! I will help you as you speak, and I will teach you what to say” (verses 11-12).

“But Moses replied, ‘Please, Lord, send someone else’” (verse 13).

The LORD's anger burns against Moses, but he gives him his brother: “Is not Aaron the Levite your brother? I know that he can speak well, and he is now on his way to meet you” (verse 14). Aaron will be Moses' spokesman, “and it will be as if you were God to him” (verse 16). Moses is to take the staff and do the signs with it (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Moses' fourth objection is about himself again. He is not a man of words. In Hebrew he calls himself heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue. The same word ‘heavy’ will later describe Pharaoh's heart. Exodus does not say what Moses' trouble was. Some think of a speech defect. Some think of a lack of confidence. Some think his Egyptian had grown rusty after so many years away.

God answers with questions. Who made the mouth? Who decides if a person can speak, hear or see? The point is that God is not limited by what Moses lacks. Then comes a promise, and in Hebrew it says, I will be with your mouth. It uses ehyeh, ‘I will be’, the word of God's name in chapter 3.

These verses must be read carefully. God says he made every person, the deaf and the hearing, the blind and the seeing. They do not say that anyone's disability is a punishment. Disability is not punishment for sin, the person's own or anyone else's. Every person, with any disability or illness, is made by God and is precious to him. No one is a mistake.

Then comes Moses' fifth answer. It is no longer a question. It is a polite refusal: send anyone but me. It is the only one of his objections that makes God angry. The Hebrew says the LORD's nose grew hot, the usual Hebrew picture for anger. But even in anger God does not replace Moses. He gives him a partner. Aaron is already on the way, and he will be glad to see his brother.

‘As if you were God to him’ does not make Moses divine. It describes a role. Moses will give Aaron the words, as God gives a prophet his words, and Aaron will speak them.
passages.later:
God promises a later prophet in the same words: “I will put My words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him” (Deuteronomy 18:18). He tells Jeremiah, “Behold, I have put My words in your mouth” (Jeremiah 1:9).

The God who asks, ‘Who gave man his mouth?’ is the God whose Son made the crowds say, “He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!” (Mark 7:37). That link is a theme, not a prediction, but it is the same God at work.

Jesus said of a man born blind, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3).
passages.asks: Moses said, ‘Send someone else’, and God gave him a brother instead of letting him go. Ask what you have refused to do because you felt you lacked something. And ask who God may have already sent to stand beside you.

passages.happening:
Moses asks his father-in-law, Jethro, to let him go back to Egypt. “Go in peace,” Jethro says (verse 18). God tells Moses, “all the men who sought to kill you are dead” (verse 19). Moses sets out with his wife and sons, “And he took the staff of God in his hand” (verse 20).

God says, “When you go back to Egypt, see that you perform before Pharaoh all the wonders that I have put within your power. But I will harden his heart so that he will not let the people go” (verse 21).

“Then tell Pharaoh that this is what the LORD says: ‘Israel is My firstborn son, and I told you to let My son go so that he may worship Me. But since you have refused to let him go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son!’” (verses 22-23).
passages.hearers:
Moses gives Jethro a modest reason for going. He says nothing about the burning bush. The shepherd's staff is now called ‘the staff of God’.

The firstborn son was the heir of the family. He received a double share of what his father left, and he carried the family's future. Pharaoh's firstborn was heir to the throne itself.

So God's message is stark. Israel is God's own son, his firstborn. Pharaoh holds God's son as a slave. ‘Let my son go so that he may worship me’ joins the book's two key verbs, ‘let go’ and ‘serve’. In Hebrew ‘worship’ here is the word for serving. Israel is to be freed from serving Pharaoh in order to serve God. If Pharaoh refuses, his own son will die. The last plague is announced before the first one falls. Everything in chapters 7 to 12 works out these two sentences.

And here, for the first time, God says he will harden Pharaoh's heart. The word here means to make strong or firm. God will make Pharaoh's will firm in its resistance.
passages.later:
Hosea remembers the exodus in the same terms: “When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son” (Hosea 11:1). Hosea looks back to the exodus, not forward. Matthew applies the line to Jesus, brought back from Egypt as a child: “Out of Egypt I called My Son” (Matthew 2:15). Most readers take Matthew to mean that Jesus is the Son in whom Israel's story is lived again and brought to its goal.

Matthew also echoes verse 19 when the angel tells Joseph, “those seeking the Child’s life are now dead” (Matthew 2:20).

Paul quotes God's word to Pharaoh in Romans 9: “I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth” (Romans 9:17).
passages.hard:
‘I will harden his heart.’ If God hardened Pharaoh's heart, how can Pharaoh be blamed?

Exodus says it in three ways. God says ahead of time that he will harden Pharaoh's heart (here and 7:3). The text says Pharaoh's heart was hard, without naming a cause (7:13). And it says Pharaoh hardened his own heart (8:15). Only from the sixth plague on does the narrator say that the LORD hardened it (9:12). Through the first five plagues, Pharaoh's own resistance comes first. The Hebrew uses three verbs for it: to make strong, to make heavy, and to make hard.

Christians read this in more than one way. Many in the Reformed tradition, following Paul in Romans 9, hold that God's sovereign purpose stands behind Pharaoh's choices without making them any less Pharaoh's own, so that he remains fully guilty. Many in the Arminian tradition, and many Jewish readers, stress that Pharaoh hardened himself first, and that God's hardening was a judgment that confirmed the road Pharaoh had already chosen. Some add a point from the verb ‘make strong’: God kept Pharaoh from simply collapsing in fear, so that his choices showed what was really in his heart.

Both readings agree on this: Pharaoh is never pictured as a man who wanted to do right and was stopped. Exodus holds God's rule and Pharaoh's guilt together, and it does not explain how. This is a question on which faithful Christians differ, and these notes take no side.
passages.asks: God calls his people ‘My firstborn son’. Ask what it means for you that God speaks of his people with a father's love, and fights for them. And ask whether there is anything in your life that holds you in a slavery God wants to set you free from.

passages.t: The night on the road, and ‘a bridegroom of blood’
passages.happening:
“Now at a lodging place along the way, the LORD met Moses and was about to kill him” (verse 24).

“But Zipporah took a flint knife, cut off her son’s foreskin, and touched it to Moses’ feet. ‘Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me,’ she said” (verse 25).

“So the LORD let him alone.” The narrator adds that when she said “bridegroom of blood,” “she was referring to the circumcision” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the most puzzling passages in the Old Testament. It is short, sudden, and strange, and the honest thing is to say plainly that it is obscure. Readers have never agreed on all its details.

Here is what the Hebrew does and does not say. It says the LORD met him and sought to kill him. It does not name who ‘him’ is. Most translations, like the BSB, take it as Moses; some readers think it was the son. The ancient Greek translation says ‘an angel of the Lord’ met him, softening it. Zipporah cuts off her son's foreskin and touches it to ‘his feet’. The BSB supplies Moses' name, but the Hebrew leaves it open. Some take ‘feet’ as a polite word for the private parts, as it sometimes is elsewhere.

Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham, to be done when a boy was eight days old (Genesis 17:10-14). Other peoples, Egyptians among them, practised a form of it. What made it Israel's was its meaning: a mark of belonging to God. Flint knives were still used for it a generation later (Joshua 5:2).

Notice where the scene is placed. It comes right after God's warning that Pharaoh's firstborn will die. Before Moses faces Egypt over its sons, his own son's life is at stake, and it is shielded by blood.
passages.later:
God's covenant with Abraham said: “But if any male is not circumcised, he will be cut off from his people; he has broken My covenant” (Genesis 17:14). The verb for Zipporah's cutting is the same verb used for being ‘cut off’ there.

Joshua circumcises the next generation with flint knives before they enter the land: “Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel once again” (Joshua 5:2).

Paul later says that what matters is a circumcision of the heart: “circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code” (Romans 2:29).
passages.hard:
Why does the LORD try to kill Moses right after sending him, and what does Zipporah's act mean? No reading settles every detail.

The most common reading, ancient and modern, is that Moses had not circumcised his son, for reasons the text does not give. The man sent to lead God's covenant people could not do so while neglecting the covenant's own sign. Zipporah does at once what Moses had left undone, and the danger lifts.

Others stress where the scene stands. Coming just after the warning that Pharaoh's firstborn will die, it shows Moses' own family under the same judgment and spared by blood, a preview of the Passover.

Many critical scholars think an older story, perhaps one that explained the phrase ‘bridegroom of blood’, has been taken up and placed here.

What the passage makes plain is this: the God who sends Moses is not a tool Moses carries in his bag. He is holy, and his covenant is not optional, even for his chosen servant. Beyond that, these notes do not claim to know more than the text says.
passages.asks: This strange night reminds every reader that God is not tame. Ask whether you have treated God's call as something you can carry on your own terms. And ask what it means that, in the danger, it was Zipporah's quick obedience that saved the day.

passages.t: Aaron meets Moses, and the people believe
passages.happening:
God tells Aaron, “Go and meet Moses in the wilderness.” Aaron goes, meets Moses “at the mountain of God and kissed him” (verse 27). Moses tells him everything (verse 28).

They gather all the elders of Israel. Aaron speaks, and Moses performs the signs, “and they believed. And when they heard that the LORD had attended to the Israelites and had seen their affliction, they bowed down and worshiped” (verses 29-31).
passages.hearers:
The Hebrew uses the same verb, ‘met’, for the LORD meeting Moses on the road in verse 24 and for Aaron meeting Moses here. The two meetings stand side by side. One brought Moses near death. The other brings his brother's embrace.

The chapter began with Moses' fear: ‘What if they do not believe me?’ It ends with the reverse: ‘and they believed’. The message they hear repeats God's words from the bush, that he has ‘attended to’ them. That is the word of Joseph's promise long ago (Genesis 50:24). The people respond as Israel would in every age: they bow down and worship.

It is a hopeful ending. The next chapter will test it hard.
passages.later:
Joseph's dying words had promised this: “God will surely visit you” (Genesis 50:24).

Psalm 105 remembers how God sent these two brothers: “He sent Moses His servant, and Aaron, whom He had chosen” (Psalm 105:26).

Hebrews sets Moses beside Jesus: “Moses was faithful as a servant in all God’s house” (Hebrews 3:5), and Christ “is faithful as the Son over God’s house” (Hebrews 3:6).
passages.asks: When the people heard that God had seen their suffering, they bowed down and worshiped, before anything had changed. Ask whether you can worship God for having seen you, even before you see the answer. And ask who you could meet and embrace, as Aaron did, to strengthen someone for a hard task.
